subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In poems about 'nature', a common idea poets explore is...
options: Nature's power, beauty or indifference compared with human concerns
questions.explain: Nature poems often weigh human experience against nature's beauty, power or indifference to draw out a theme.

questions.q: What major building project causes hardship and dispute among the animals?
questions.explain: The windmill, repeatedly built and destroyed, becomes a symbol of the animals' exploited labour.

questions.q: How does Napoleon finally seize sole power over the farm?
options: He sets his trained dogs on Snowball to chase him away
questions.explain: Napoleon unleashes the fierce dogs he reared in secret to expel Snowball.

questions.q: A rhyming couplet at the end of a poem can be used to...
options: Indicate the poem is free verse
Provide a neat, emphatic sense of closure or a final twist
questions.explain: A closing couplet often rounds off the poem with a memorable, resolved or pointed final statement.

questions.q: Repetition of a key word or phrase in a poem usually serves to...
options: Signal the end of the anthology
Emphasise an idea or emotion and create rhythm or insistence
questions.explain: Repetition foregrounds an idea, building emphasis, rhythm or a sense of obsession depending on context.

questions.q: How do poets commonly present the theme of 'power'?
options: Often by exposing how power is temporary, corrupting or undermined by time/nature
By showing it as permanent and unchallengeable always
questions.explain: Many power poems explore its fragility, arrogance or eventual decay, contrasting human power with time or nature.

questions.q: Animal Farm is an allegory for which historical event?
questions.explain: Orwell's fable allegorises the Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalinist tyranny.

questions.q: When a poem about 'memory' moves between past and present tense, this often...
options: Means the poem is a ballad
Blurs the boundary between then and now, showing how the past persists
questions.explain: Shifting tense can dramatise how memory intrudes on the present, keeping the past emotionally alive.

questions.q: In poems exploring 'the effects of war', poets often present...
options: Only patriotic triumph with no complexity
The physical and psychological suffering and lasting trauma of conflict
questions.explain: War poetry frequently foregrounds suffering, trauma and the human cost rather than uncomplicated glory.

questions.q: If a poem's lines follow the pattern da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, the metre is...
questions.explain: Five iambic feet per line is iambic pentameter, the most common metre in English poetry.

questions.q: When a poem about 'loss' uses the present tense to describe a person now gone, the effect is often to...
options: Confuse the reader for no reason
Keep the memory vivid and immediate, as if the person is still present
Prove the poem is a sonnet
questions.explain: Present tense can make memory feel alive and ongoing, emphasising how loss keeps the absent person emotionally present.

questions.q: A poem spoken in the voice of a single fictional speaker, revealing their character to a silent listener, is a...
questions.explain: A dramatic monologue uses one speaker's voice to expose their personality, often unintentionally, to an implied listener.
